analysis.title: Consumer Checkpoint: Spending season
key_insights: BofA total card spending per household rose 5.8% YoY in October, down from 6.2% in September. Spending excluding gasoline rose 4.6% YoY, down from 5.1%.
Seasonally adjusted total card spending rose 0.1% MoM in October, with or without gas. BofA reads this as momentum staying positive.
Services contributed 2.5pp to YoY card spending growth in October, down from 2.7pp in September. Retail contributed 1.2pp, down from 1.6pp in September and 2pp at the summer peak.

October YoY spending growth was 7.8% for airlines, 4.6% for general merchandise, 2.8% for restaurants, 2.1% for leisure and 2.1% for lodging. Clothing slowed to 1.0%. Miscellaneous stores (8.4%) and non-store retailers (13.5%) accelerated modestly from September.
Lower-income households led total card spending growth at 5.9% YoY in October, ahead of the top 5% at 5.7%. Middle- and higher-income households were each up around 5%.
The top 5% of earners still lead discretionary spending growth, but the gap to other cohorts is the smallest since May 2025.

After-tax wage growth is 4.7% YoY for lower-income households, just below 4% for middle-income and 3.4% for higher-income households. BofA says the labor market is a primary driver of lower-income spending strength.
Card spending growth has outpaced after-tax wage growth for every income cohort for five months. BofA calls this mostly a base effect, because wages are a larger dollar base than spending.

The gap between spending and wage growth is largest for the top 5%, which BofA attributes partly to wealth effects. BofA says recent stock market volatility needs close attention, but spending may stay robust with only small to modest equity pullbacks.

Holiday item spending is running well above 2025 levels, led by online purchases. Online holiday spending is running 3pp above overall holiday spending, while average transaction value is below 2025 levels. BofA suggests consumers are shifting to cheaper items.

November and December typically account for at least one in five dollars of annual revenue in general merchandise, electronics and clothing. Jewelry generates nearly a quarter of its annual revenue in that period.

BofA's holiday survey (Sept 10-12, 2,062 respondents) suggests most holiday shopping will happen later this year, which counters the view that current strength is only a pull-forward. About 46% of lower-income respondents plan to spend less.

A higher share of households in every income cohort pay off their full credit card balance each month than in 2019 and 2025. Card utilization for households carrying a balance is near 2019 levels, except for lower-income households.

Signs of stress at the margins: the share of households making only minimum card payments is rising in 2026, though more slowly than last year. The share of 401(k) participants taking hardship distributions has risen slightly for two consecutive quarters, including Q3 2026.

The tax-refund boost to deposits earlier in 2026 has run its course. Deposits remain above pre-pandemic inflation-adjusted levels in all income cohorts, which BofA says leaves a buffer for holiday spending.

sector_views.rationale: Holiday item spending is strong and online-led, but discretionary growth cooled in most categories and average ticket sizes are falling.

macro_indicators.indicator: BofA total card spending per household
macro_indicators.interpretation: Down from +6.2% in September but still close to the strong rates seen since spring 2026.

macro_indicators.indicator: BofA card spending per household excluding gasoline
macro_indicators.interpretation: Down from +5.1% in September, so the slowdown is not only a gasoline effect.

macro_indicators.indicator: BofA seasonally adjusted total card spending
macro_indicators.interpretation: Small positive monthly gain, with or without gasoline. BofA reads momentum as still positive.
Fastest of the income groups, ahead of the top 5% at +5.7%.
Strongest of the cohorts and a main support for lower-income spending.
Slowest of the cohorts, so spending growth for this group depends more on wealth effects.

risk_factors: Equity market declines could reduce wealth-effect spending among the top 5% of households.
Rising minimum credit card payments and a slight rise in 401(k) hardship distributions point to stress at the margins.
About 46% of lower-income holiday survey respondents plan to spend less this year.
Average transaction values for holiday items are below 2025 levels, and durables transactions fell YoY in October.
Price increases elsewhere may be pushing consumers toward cheaper items.

tension_points.bull_case: Holiday item spending is running well above 2025 levels, led by online purchases. Survey respondents lean toward shopping later in the season, so the early strength may not be a pull-forward. Deposits and full-balance payoff rates are healthy.
tension_points.bear_case: Average transaction values are below 2025 levels, consistent with trading down. About 46% of lower-income respondents plan to spend less, and minimum payments and 401(k) hardship distributions are edging up.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Equity market declines larger than the 'small to modest pullbacks' BofA says spending can absorb, which would hit top 5% wealth-effect spending.

theme_stances.key_argument: Card spending growth remains solid and has converged across income groups, supported by after-tax wage growth.
theme_stances.evidence: Consumer spending remains solid, even as momentum moderates.

theme_stances.key_argument: Top 5% spending outpaces their wage growth partly due to wealth effects, and spending may hold with only small to modest equity pullbacks.
